newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Stiff upper lip Clarke defends British colonial past.
newsitem.headline: Stiff upper lip Clarke defends British colonial past.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke resorted to the fabled stiff upper lip to fend off barbs about his country's colonial past at an international financial conference in Hong Kong on Friday.
"Britain's record on human rights in the colonies has been better than that of some of the governments that are ruling now," Clarke told a news conference.

Clarke was answering a question about statements attributed to Malaysian Finance and Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who had said Britain's 200-year record in its former colonies gave it no right to talk about human rights.
Malaysia was once part of the empire in which colonial Britain held sway.
Clarke said the British era of colonialism was before his time and he was not shedding tears over the loss of empire.
He said that Britain had tried to remain positively engaged with former colonies.

"If you look at the countries in which we were formally a colonial power, you will see that we have good relations," he said. "We left behind a better situation than we found in almost every country that we found (colonised)."
Britain is quitting Hong Kong, its last colonial possession in Asia, on July 1 and handing it back to China, from where it was prised more than 150 years ago.
Earlier on Friday, Clarke had said Britain would be keeping a close eye on Hong Kong's freedoms.
After the Hong Kong handover, Britain will have only 12 small colonies left, the remnants of a global empire over which the sun, once, never set.
